boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Fort Sumter record (April 12-14, 1861) in Operations in Charleston Harbor [April 1861]. The December 1860-April 1861 occupation and siege of the fort, the firing on the Star of the West and the relief expeditions are context. Campaign-wide movements, reinforcements, returns and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. Imported numerical estimates remain unchanged; this pass does not validate them as simultaneous opening forces.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads 'Regiments: 580 total (US 80; CS 500)' and the live page gives the same totals. Nicolay counts the garrison as nine officers, sixty-eight non-commissioned officers and privates, eight musicians and forty-three non-combatant workmen, 128 souls in all, against a Confederate volunteer force of four to six thousand supporting the batteries, and puts the armaments at forty-eight guns in the fort and forty-seven in the besieging works, seventeen of them mortars. Anderson reports only 'my little force' and the fire of seventeen 10-inch mortars and batteries of heavy guns.
claims.rationale: Figures differ in population: the frozen 80 and 500, Nicolay's garrison with and without workmen, and his range for the force supporting the batteries; gun counts are not personnel. None is adopted as a matched opening strength.

claims.value: Anderson says he accepted terms with four barrels and three cartridges of powder only available and no provisions remaining but pork, the magazine surrounded by flames. Nicolay says supplies from the city were prohibited from April 2, the last barrel of flour had been issued two or three days before the bombardment, the garrison's 700 cartridges ran short with only six needles to sew cartridge-bags, and the relief expedition could not succor the fort.
claims.rationale: Supply state from an interested report and a history; no ordnance or subsistence return inspected.

claims.value: Nicolay says Lincoln's notice that an attempt would be made to supply the fort with provisions only was read to Pickens and Beauregard on the evening of April 8; that Anderson's remark that the garrison would be starved out in a few days, repeated to Beauregard, gave the impression that he wished to capitulate; and that Wigfall, without authority, offered terms on April 13. NPS dates Beauregard's demand for surrender to April 10; Nicolay says Beauregard was instructed on the 10th and sent the demand at two o'clock on April 11, and Anderson refers to terms offered on the 11th.
claims.rationale: Attributed knowledge from a history; the date of the demand differs between the summary and the history and report.

claims.value: The frozen commanders are Brigadier General P.G.T. Beauregard and Major Robert Anderson, matching the live page. Nicolay says Beauregard was sent on March 1 to direct military affairs and complete the preparations for capture; that Anderson withdrew his men from the barbette guns; that Captain Abner Doubleday fired the fort's first gun; and that Beauregard agreed to Anderson's proposal. Anderson says he accepted Beauregard's terms.
claims.rationale: Command roles from a history and an interested report; neither listed commander receives automatic sole credit.

claims.value: The frozen result reads Confederate victory and the live result Indecisive. NPS says Anderson surrendered at 2:30 p.m. on April 13 and evacuated the next day. Anderson says he defended the fort for thirty-four hours and marched out on the afternoon of Sunday the 14th with colors flying, saluting his flag with fifty guns; Nicolay gives thirty-six hours of bombardment from half-past four on April 12 and the evacuation at noon on April 14.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit. The live 'Indecisive' is not adopted over the frozen result; hour and duration differences are preserved.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads None; the live field reads 15 (US 11; CS 4). NPS says there were no casualties during the bombardment and that one artillerist was killed and three wounded, one mortally, by a premature explosion during the salute on April 14. Anderson says no one was seriously injured by the enemy's fire and that one man was killed and two seriously and three slightly wounded while saluting; Nicolay says the bombardment cost no life in the garrison.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. The salute accident follows the surrender and is not a combat loss; the live 15 has no inspected basis.

open_questions: Beauregard's reports (No. 8), Foster's engineer journal (No. 7), Fox's report on the relief expedition (No. 5), the South Carolina subordinate reports (Nos. 9-28) and Anderson's promised detailed report remain deferred.
The date of Beauregard's demand (April 10 in NPS, April 11 in Nicolay and Anderson) and the hour of surrender and evacuation remain unreconciled.

NPS/CWSAC is one family. John G. Nicolay's The Outbreak of Rebellion (Scribner, 1881) is a retrospective history written, by its preface, largely from the Official War Records for 1861; it quotes Anderson's correspondence and is not independent of the Anderson family. Anderson's April 18 telegram and April 19, 1861 report (Official Records Series I, Volume I, No. 6) are one family of interested Union accounts. The Official Records volume is a shared container, not an additional witness. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
